interviewQuestions.question: What's the practical difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden, and why do people mix them up?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as identity versus permission, and lead with the fix each one implies. **401** means the server doesn't know who's asking — credentials missing, expired, or invalid — and the fix is to authenticate (log in, refresh the token). **403** means the server knows exactly who's asking, and that identity simply isn't allowed to do this — re-authenticating changes nothing, because the problem isn't who you are, it's what you're permitted to do.

Concretely: hit an admin endpoint with no token at all, you get 401. Hit it logged in as a normal user, you get 403. A client that treats both the same way — say, redirecting to a login page on either — will loop a properly-authenticated user back to a login screen forever when what they actually need is different permissions, which is a real, shippable bug.

The confusion happens partly because the spec itself is a little unhelpful here: `401 Unauthorized` is poorly named (it's really "Unauthenticated"), and plenty of production APIs return 403 for both cases anyway to avoid leaking whether a resource exists at all — a deliberate trade-off between correctness of the status code and information disclosure. I'd mention that nuance if asked to design the response codes myself: strict correctness says 401 vs 403, but a security-conscious API sometimes prefers 404 or a blanket 403 to avoid confirming a resource's existence to an unauthorized caller.

**Testing:** whether you can map each code to the right client-side fix, and whether you're aware of the information-disclosure trade-off senior API designers actually weigh.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: 401 vs 403

interviewQuestions.question: Why does HTTP/1.1's persistent connection support matter so much for real-world page load performance?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Under HTTP/1.0's default, every single resource on a page — the HTML, then each CSS file, each image, each script — meant tearing down and re-establishing a fresh TCP connection (and a TLS handshake on top, if HTTPS), which is pure round-trip overhead before a single useful byte moves.

HTTP/1.1 defaults to **keep-alive**: one TCP connection stays open and carries a sequence of requests and responses. A page with 30 assets pays the connection-setup cost once instead of 30 times. On a network with a realistic 50-100ms round trip, that's the difference between roughly 3-6 extra seconds of pure handshake overhead and near-zero — a very visible difference in page load time, especially on mobile or long-distance links.

The catch that makes this a good follow-up topic: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive still processes requests on a connection **serially by default** (or with limited pipelining that browsers mostly disabled due to head-of-line blocking bugs), so browsers historically worked around it by opening **multiple parallel connections per host** (commonly 6) to get concurrency — itself a workaround with costs, since each connection still needs its own TCP/TLS setup and competes for the same bandwidth. This exact limitation is what HTTP/2's multiplexing was built to remove: true concurrent requests over a *single* connection, no parallel-connection workaround needed. See [HTTP/2 Multiplexing](http2-multiplexing) for how that evolved.

**Testing:** whether you connect a protocol default (keep-alive) to its measurable real-world performance impact, and whether you know its follow-on limitation that motivated HTTP/2.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why keep-alive matters

interviewQuestions.question: HTTP is described as stateless. How do real applications implement 'the user is logged in' on top of a stateless protocol?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The protocol genuinely has no memory — the server processing request #2 has no built-in way to know it came from the same client as request #1. Real apps fake continuity on top using two main patterns, and I'd contrast them because the trade-off comes up constantly.

**Cookie-based sessions:** on login, the server creates a session record (in memory, Redis, a database) keyed by a random session ID, and sends that ID back via `Set-Cookie`. The browser automatically attaches it on every subsequent request via the `Cookie` header, and the server looks up the session to know who's asking. The server holds the actual state; the cookie is just a pointer to it — which makes revoking a session trivial (delete the record) but requires either a shared session store or sticky routing across multiple app servers.

**Token-based (JWT):** the token itself carries the claims (user ID, roles, expiry), cryptographically signed, and the client sends it in an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. The server verifies the signature and trusts the contents without a database lookup — genuinely stateless, which is why this scales better across many servers with no shared session store. The cost: revoking a single token before its expiry is hard, because there's no central record to delete; you either keep expiries short or maintain a denylist, which quietly reintroduces the state you were trying to avoid.

In both cases, HTTP itself stays exactly as stateless as ever — the application layer is doing all the work of simulating continuity, which is the point of the question.

**Testing:** whether you can name both patterns and articulate the actual trade-off (revocability vs statelessness), not just that 'cookies exist.'
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Statelessness in practice

interviewQuestions.question: You're designing a payment API. A client's POST to charge a card times out with no response. What do you tell them about retrying, and how does HTTP's method semantics factor in?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd start from what actually happened, which the client can't know for certain: the request may have never reached the server, reached it and failed before charging, or **reached it, charged the card, and the response was lost on the way back**. A timeout is silence, not a no.

This is exactly why `POST` being non-idempotent matters in practice, not just as trivia: blindly retrying a `POST` on timeout risks a double charge, because the server has no way to tell "this is the same logical request retried" from "this is a second, separate purchase." The fix isn't to avoid retries — networks fail and retries are necessary for reliability — it's to make the operation **idempotent at the application layer** even though the HTTP verb isn't: the client generates a unique `Idempotency-Key` (a UUID) per logical charge attempt and sends it with every retry of that same attempt. The server persists which keys it has already processed and, on a repeat, returns the original result instead of charging again. Stripe's API popularized exactly this pattern for this exact reason.

I'd also point out the design symmetry: `PUT` and `DELETE` don't need this because they're idempotent by definition — replaying "set the balance to $50" or "delete order 42" twice has the same end state as once. It's specifically the non-idempotent, side-effecting `POST` that needs an idempotency layer bolted on, and payments are the canonical example of where getting this wrong is expensive.

**Testing:** whether you connect the protocol's idempotency guarantees to a real production failure mode, and whether you know the actual mitigation (idempotency keys), not just "don't retry POSTs."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Idempotency in production
